title: How Market Position Shapes Credit Card Interest Rates - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed/Minneapolis Fed research on 14 million new credit cards finds lenders pass through ~20% less of funding-cost declines in markets where they hold large share, so similar borrowers get different APRs from the same lender.

insights.claim: Across 960 defined nationwide credit card markets, average APRs among finely matched account groups correlate 54% positively with lender market share, and the relation holds after controlling for borrower and bank characteristics.
insights.speaker: Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli
insights.so_what: Concentration is associated with higher card pricing.

insights.claim: When the federal funds rate fell unexpectedly by 25bp in January 2008, the same lender's pass-through to new-card APRs was 20% lower in its high-share markets (top 30% of shares) than in low-share markets, i.e. about 2 percentage points less cut per 1pp change in the risk-free rate on a 10% APR.
insights.speaker: Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli
insights.so_what: Fed rate cuts transmit less to card borrowers where lenders hold market power.
insights.locator: Lenders Pass Through Less Where Their Shares Are Larger

insights.claim: The result is not unique to January 2008; it remains sizable across all large 2008 surprises, and across 2008-2019 events is smaller but statistically significant, using roughly 14 million new accounts.
insights.speaker: Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli
insights.so_what: Pattern is robust across events and borrower groups.
insights.locator: Lenders Pass Through Less Where Their Shares Are Larger

insights.claim: Borrowers with similar credit score, income and card type taking cards from the same nationwide lender can face different APRs depending on that lender's share in their specific market segment.
insights.speaker: Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli
insights.so_what: Market-power pricing implies monetary-policy transmission is uneven; relevant for card issuer margins and regulation.

source_meta.author: Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli
